title: AI Boom Forces Massive Investment in Power Grids Worldwide
summary: The information technology industry is driving massive growth in global electricity demand, which is set to rise by more than 10,000 TWh over the next ten years. For this electricity to reach demand hubs, grids around the world will need urgent upgrades. The big question is who will pay for it. body: Thanksgiving Gas Prices Could Break a Record Despite Recent Plunge What I Cover Irina Slav has been writing about global energy markets since 2007, covering the oil and gas industry, energy security, commodities, and the… The information technology industry is driving massive growth in global electricity demand, which is set to rise by more than 10,000 TWh over the next ten years. For this electricity to reach demand hubs, grids around the world will need urgent upgrades. In its World Energy Outlook released this week, the International Energy Agency once again joined the growing chorus of forecasters warning that data centers are becoming a major drain on electricity supply. Some of these warnings and community opposition to new facilities that may bring their electricity bills higher helped tip the midterm scales in Democrats’ favor. Others are casting doubts about the AI revolution's potential for success if data center operators cannot secure enough electricity for all their planned facilities. The IEA noted the importance of keeping electricity affordable as pro-transition governments try to boost the share of electricity in final energy consumption. “Successful electrification means keeping electricity available and affordable, putting the emphasis on effective use and expansion of grids, and greater operational flexibility in power systems,” the International Energy Agency wrote in the executive summary of its report. It then went on to add that while AI is widely expected to help with things like energy efficiency and grid optimization, “for the moment, surging demand from data centres is amplifying strains in some markets and supply chains.” The financial side of the energy problem with data centers is the most serious one. Net-zero ambitions already required massive spend on new transmission lines before the AI craze began. Now, the tab is just going to go higher as data centers join other demand centers that need to be supplied with reliable, hopefully low-carbon electricity, per the IEA’s and net-zero governments’ agenda. Meanwhile, as it emerges that data center operators tend to split the grid connection bill generously with nearby residents, opposition is likely to grow as well. Related: China’s Oil Imports from Persian Gulf Jump to Wartime High A study from Cornell University this month revealed that wholesale prices for electricity across four regions in the U.S. rose because of demand from data centers. However, the study also found that these data centers’ operators only paid for 38% of the infrastructure costs related to their facilities’ connection to and use of the grid. The remainder fell on local communities. In money terms, data center operators paid $3.12 billion, and households paid $5.13 billion. The Wall Street Journal reported this week that there were some 58 GW in new data centers under construction across the United States, citing data from Cleanview. That total represented 577 locations, whose demand for electricity the WSJ compared to six times the electricity demand of New York City at its peak. A fifth of that total is being built in Texas--but Texas just got a change of the guard, and the newcomers are not big fans of data centers. “We need an immediate moratorium on data centers to last until the legislature can meet to put in place real protections so Texans can have a seat at the table to decide if and how data centers come into their communities,” Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa’s campaign website said before the election. On that, she was in agreement with predecessor Greg Abbott, who earlier this year banned new data center approvals to investigate whether they were having a negative impact on energy prices and other issues. Whether the data center building boom slows or not, there is already plenty of new demand for electricity coming from these facilities and, in countries run by strong pro-transition politicians, the drive to replace baseload electricity with wind and solar continues

title: India's GDP Growth Draws Global Attention as Trump Cites Economic Success to Criticise US Fed - Khalsa Vox
body: India's strong economic growth has found a prominent mention in American political discourse, with US President Donald Trump highlighting the country's 7 per cent GDP expansion while criticising the Federal Reserve's interest rate policies. Speaking at a White House press conference on Friday, November 20, Trump pointed to India's economic performance as an example of how favourable borrowing conditions could support growth. His remarks placed India's economic momentum at the centre of a debate over US monetary policy. "If you look at India, they have low interest rates, and they have a 7 per cent GDP," Trump said, contrasting the Indian economy with the United States. The American President argued that the US could achieve significantly higher growth if its central bank reduced borrowing costs. He suggested that American GDP growth could potentially reach 15 to 20 per cent, although such figures represented his own projections rather than established economic forecasts. Trump also accused the Federal Reserve of being politically influenced, claiming that interest rates remained unnecessarily high despite positive economic indicators. For India, the comparison marks a notable moment of international recognition, with the world's largest economy looking towards India's growth performance during a discussion about its own economic prospects. India has remained among the fastest-growing major economies, supported by domestic economic activity and its expanding presence in global markets. Its growth trajectory has attracted international attention as major economies navigate inflationary pressures, uncertain trade conditions and changing monetary policies. Trump's reference is particularly significant because India was presented as a positive economic comparison rather than merely as an emerging market. The remarks underscore the growing visibility of Indian economic performance in global policy discussions. However, differences between the two economies remain substantial. Interest rate decisions depend on inflation, employment conditions, financial stability and other domestic factors. Lower borrowing costs alone do not guarantee faster economic growth. The Federal Reserve continues to face inflationary pressures, with US annual personal consumption expenditures inflation reportedly reaching 3.6 per cent in September, above its 2 per cent target. Nevertheless, the White House remarks have brought renewed attention to India's economic trajectory. As India strengthens its position in the international economic landscape, Trump's invocation of its growth rate reflects how the country's performance is increasingly becoming part of conversations about global competitiveness and economic policymaking. The comparison also reinforces India's rising profile as a major economy whose growth figures command attention beyond its borders.

title: US President Trump lauds India’s economic growth & low interest rates - The Indian Awaaz
body: US President Donald Trump has praised India’s low interest rates and strong economic growth. He cited India as an example while criticising the US Federal Reserve for damaging the American economy by keeping interest rates high despite strong economic performance. Mr Trump made the comparison at a news conference in Washington last night after returning from a four-day visit to Asia. Referring to India’s economic growth of around seven per cent, President Trump argued that the US economy, currently growing at around four per cent, could expand by 14 to 20 per cent if the Federal Reserve lowered borrowing costs instead of keeping interest rates high. He also said that the United States should be able to borrow money at lower interest rates than any other country. Mr Trump accused the Federal Reserve of taking a political approach to monetary policy and keeping borrowing costs high despite strong economic indicators. The US President further claimed that a 1 percentage point cut in interest rates could save the country 650 billion dollars in debt payments. He also highlighted rising investments in manufacturing, saying factory activity had expanded for ten consecutive months and investment in new equipment had increased by 21 per cent this year. Mr Trump credited his tariff policies with encouraging companies such as Audi and Toyota to invest in manufacturing in the United States. He also pointed to falling oil and petrol prices as signs of economic improvement. He said future petrol prices could depend, in part, on a possible agreement between the United States and Iran. The US Federal Reserve determines interest rates based on economic conditions, particularly inflation and employment, with the twin objectives of maintaining price stability and supporting maximum employment.

title: Nvidia Stock: 5 Reasons the AI Trade Has Only Begun - I/O Fund
body: This week, Nvidia dispelled fears of the AI trade slowing with one simple number; fiscal 2028 revenue growth is guided to be 75% up from 70% despite a higher FY27 revenue base. Vera Rubin generated $20 billion in revenue in its first quarter of production shipments, which is Nvidia’s fastest ramp ever. The Q4 guide is softer than it appears as it includes an extra week. If we adjust to a 13-week quarter, it works out to $121 billion or roughly 4% sequential growth after three quarters of 20% sequential growth. The guide excludes $2.4 billion in licensed Hopper sales to China that contributed to Q3. Don’t sweat it, though; we’ve been here before. When Nvidia transitions between product generations, the market typically panics as it reads the lull as a permanent slowdown. In fact, some of my very best AI entries have occurred during the pause between generations. As of now, Rubin’s first quarter is nearly double Blackwell’s at $20 billion compared to $11 billion, respectively. Management also stated the ramp is “off to an extraordinary start. During the Blackwell transition, sequential growth slowed to 12% in each of the first two quarters of the ramp, then to 6% in Q2 when H20 sales from China went to zero . After that, sales re-accelerated to 22% and 19% QoQ. Margins are the weaker part of the story, but you’d have to be living under a rock not to expect memory costs to weigh on profitability . Gross margin is expected to fall from 74.9% to 71%-72% in Q4, which the CFO said was a bottom with margins expected to return to 72%-73%. Now that we’ve gotten some of the obligatory earnings coverage out of the way, let’s talk about what’s really on everyone’s minds – is the AI trade over? Or perhaps equally concerning, is AI slowing to the point the glory years are behind us? Before we discuss the facts, I would encourage investors to pay close attention to who is spreading fear, uncertainty and doubt when the underlying fundamentals remain strong. Valid concerns are worth considering, but investors should deeply question why the concerns are brought up after a steep selloff rather than before it. Psychology is a major component of successful investing, and there is not a more important time to protect your mindset than when stock prices are at a multi-year low. Case in point, you’d have to go back at least 10 years to find Nvidia trading this low; therefore, it’s reasonable that many years go by until investors see some of these valuations again. With that in mind, below are five reasons we believe the current panic may be presenting investors with a rare buying opportunity, rather than signaling the end of the AI trade. The defining characteristic of the AI infrastructure cycle continues to be demand greatly exceeding supply. AI suppliers are building against contracted demand, which is distinguished from previous tech bubbles when suppliers were building on speculative demand. For example, SK Hynix has stated they are effectively sold out through 2029. Nvidia’s supply-related commitments rose to $390 billion, which reflects the sheer scale of supply chain expansion as this is up 3X over two quarters, given commitments were $119 billion in the April quarter. Another indication of the strong demand from Nvidia’s report was the statement that cloud industry backlog increased from $2 trillion to $2.5 trillion. The 25% sequential increase reinforces a significant step-up in cloud customers’ future demand, supported by multiyear visibility. Here is what was stated on the earnings call by CFO Collette Kress: “Our hyperscale customers’ cloud revenue growth accelerated for the sixth consecutive quarter. Cloud industry backlog now sits at $2.5 trillion, up from $2 trillion just three months ago, underscoring the significant multi-year opportunity ahead of our partners and of NVIDIA.” Nvidia reported that token prices have declined 60% since May, yet rather than weaken demand for compute, lower prices are helping to accelerate consumption. title: Peterson: Nvidia’s leadership crisis tests the chipmaker’s role as the ‘central bank of AI’
summary: The tech giant's web of ties to other companies is raising the possibility that it could do far-reaching economic and financial damage.
body: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang 's shock resignation is raising a worrying question: Could trouble at the chipmaker spread through the tightly connected financial network Nvidia has built to support the artificial intelligence boom? Follow CNBC's live coverage of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's resignation Serious problems with Nvidia could do far-reaching economic and financial damage. The company has made hundreds of billions of dollars in financial commitments to other firms to help the industry grow, earning it the nickname the "central bank of AI." The Federal Reserve and other financial institutions are closely watching the AI buildout to monitor for the possibility that an unexpected event could destabilize the global financial system. Even back in July Fed officials were discussing the possibility of a "broad-based repricing of assets" in the event of problems in the AI sector. A rerun of the 2007-2008 financial crisis isn't likely, according to analysts and current and former financial officials. Nvidia isn't "too big to fail in a bank sense at all," said Sheila Bair, a former government regulator who ran the Federal Deposit Insurance Corp. Unlike a troubled bank, Nvidia isn't vulnerable to a sudden loss of confidence and would still produce a product customers want to buy even if something went wrong. And its massive equity gives it a cushion. But regulators need to watch carefully for exposure by the banks and the wider financial system to Nvidia and other firms like it, Bair said. "Nvidia going down would be a pretty seismic event," she said. Investors still have high hopes for Nvidia, which reports earnings on Tuesday. Analysts expect its revenue to more than double in the current fiscal year, and then to roughly double again over the following two years, according to LSEG data. But Huang's exit from the company Thursday following a pair of extramarital affairs, including one with a woman The New York Times reported was suspected of spying for China, makes the company's fate extraordinarily hard to predict. Huang had led the company since co-founding it in 1993. Nvidia didn't respond to a request for comment. The company named CFO Colette Kress as interim CEO. Nvidia's stock fell 33% from its Oct. 6 peak through Thursday morning. Still, people who closely track the financial flows underlying AI say that even sharper losses by Nvidia likely wouldn't trigger the kind of systemic problems that regulators guard against. And yet the risks flowing from AI are keeping some finance officials up at night. They are watching for the possibility that many of the factors that have helped the AI boom could reverse simultaneously. If the value of Nvidia's GPU chips fell, for instance, it could prompt investors to ask whether companies that borrowed money to buy them would be able to pay off their debts. In that case, the financial assistance big tech firms have extended to others in the industry could suddenly become drags on their growth. Tech companies would have credit problems at the same time that their equity is falling. Problems among giant tech firms wouldn't stay contained to tech investors' portfolios, but could cause problems across the economy. "I think that's a real concern because both the economy and financial markets are standing on the same leg, which means a drawdown could have reinforcing effects between the two," said Jason Wu, an assistant director at the International Monetary Fund who oversees the Global Markets Analysis unit. Wu was the lead author of a chapter of the IMF's Global Financial Stability report published in October that warned about the potential for growing leverage among AI firms and investors to trigger broader problems. The so-called hyperscalers — the biggest tech firms — have grown from just 1% of bond issuance in the $15 trillion investment-grade debt market to 10% in just two years. title: Wall Street stays bearish after gold’s slide to $3,500, Main Street pessimism deepens ahead of holiday week - Kitco
body: (Kitco News) – Gold prices suffered another brutal weekly decline as increasingly hawkish Federal Reserve rate expectations, surging Treasury yields, and a stronger U.S. dollar overwhelmed safe-haven demand, while a deepening technology-led equity selloff triggered widespread liquidations and drove the precious metal to its lowest level in over a year. Spot gold kicked off the week trading at $3,869.30 per ounce on Sunday evening, and the yellow metal briefly attempted to stabilize following the previous week's sharp decline, with prices setting their weekly high at $3,901.40 per ounce on Monday. But the recovery quickly faded as markets continued to price in another Fed rate hike in December, while persistent inflation concerns and lingering tensions surrounding Iran and the Strait of Hormuz provided little support. Selling pressure intensified Tuesday after October retail sales rose just 0.2%, while stronger core spending failed to ease concerns about inflation. Gold broke decisively below $3,800 on Wednesday as the dollar strengthened, and the decline accelerated after the minutes from the Fed's October meeting showed policymakers remained firmly committed to further tightening, with some officials considering a larger 50-basis-point increase in December. The metal continued falling Thursday even after initial jobless claims rose to 203,000 and the Philadelphia Fed manufacturing index declined sharply to 6.3, as elevated input price pressures reinforced expectations for additional rate hikes. Selling then accelerated Friday as the technology-led equity rout deepened and investors liquidated precious-metals positions to cover losses elsewhere. Spot gold ultimately set its weekly low at $3,502.93 per ounce just before 2 pm ET on Friday, before a late push saw the yellow metal gain $35 of separation heading into the weekly close. The latest Kitco News Weekly Gold Survey showed Wall Street sentiment still deep in bearish territory following gold’s slide to $3,500, while Main Street bulls weakened further as the yellow metal’s selloff accelerated. “Gold, basis spot, approached my $3500 target today,” said Marc Chandler, managing director at Bannockburn Global Forex. “A break of it could spur losses to $3430-$3450. However, with falling stocks and oil taking pushing rates lower, I am looking for some kind of reversal pattern to suggest a low is in place. It has not traded above the previous session’s high since Nov 9. Should it now, it could be an early sign of bottom.” “Up,” said Rich Checkan, president and COO of Asset Strategies International. “The selling in gold is so overdone, we most certainly should head higher in the coming week. However, since this selling is likely the result of margin call selling to shore up positions in leveraged equities accounts, if the tech and finance bleeding continues in the stock market, we may still see lower prices for gold.” “Higher Treasury yields, a stronger U.S. dollar, and increased expectations of an interest rate hike at the December FOMC meeting have all contributed to gold’s demise… along with the margin call selling,” Checkan noted. “But those factors have no doubt been priced in at this point.” “Down, said Darin Newsom, senior market analyst at Barchart.com. “Do I think gold should be going up? Fundamentally, yes. But based on my Market Rule #1: Don’t get crossways with the trend; with trend defined as simply “price direction over time”, then I have to stick with gold continuing to move lower until proven otherwise. What about Market Rule #6 (out of 7), ‘Fundamentals win in the end’? Eventually, fundamentals (central bank buying) could carry the day, but not necessarily short-term.” “Neutral,” said Adam Button, head of currency strategy at investingLive. “It's been a tough month for gold. title: Solar makers cut silver use by a fifth as the gold/silver ratio climbs to a one-year high of 86 - CEO Economy
body: The Silver Institute expects demand to fall 5% this year, and silver's drop to about $41 has pushed the gold/silver ratio to 85.8, from 45.4 in January. Global silver demand is set to fall 5% this year to 1.08 billion ounces, as solar panel makers use less of the metal and jewelry buyers retreat, according to an interim review published by the Silver Institute and the consultancy Metals Focus on Nov. 12. The market is still forecast to record a sixth straight annual deficit, but a smaller one, of 35 million ounces, against 54 million ounces in 2025. Industry is the biggest source of silver demand, and it is shrinking this year. Industrial use is expected to drop 3% to 640 million ounces, though that is still about 22% above 2019. The decline comes almost entirely from photovoltaics. Silver used in solar cells is estimated to fall by about 20% this year, Kitco News reported, and the institute said solar installations fell short of expectations, especially in China. "I would actually say that the record level of solar demand is behind us, and it will continue to weaken," Philip Newman, managing director of Metals Focus, said, according to Miningmx. Solar accounted for 55% of the growth in silver demand over the past five years, and analysts at BMO said it could give up about half of those gains by 2030, Miningmx reported. Other industrial uses are still growing. Demand excluding photovoltaics is expected to rise 4.5% to 492 million ounces, with automotive demand described as resilient in the institute's release. Consumers and investors are also pulling back. Jewelry demand is forecast to fall 22% and silverware 17%. Bar and coin demand is expected to slip 2% to 215 million ounces, with US retail investment at its lowest since 2010, Reuters reported. Silver held in exchange-traded products stood at 1.25 billion ounces on Nov. 3, down 55 million ounces for the year, and Metals Focus expects net outflows of 45 million ounces in 2026 after 278 million ounces of inflows in 2025. On the supply side, mined output is expected to dip 0.5% to 834 million ounces and recycling to rise 6% to 210 million ounces. The institute estimates the market has been short by a cumulative 746 million ounces from 2021 to 2026. The price has fallen much faster than gold's. Silver closed near $41.19 an ounce on Friday, Nov. 20, its lowest since September 2025 and about two-thirds below its record of $121.65 on Jan. 26, according to Trading Economics and the Silver Institute. That pushed the gold/silver ratio, the number of ounces of silver that one ounce of gold buys, to 85.8 on Nov. 20, a 52-week high, according to Bullion Trading LLC, which tracks the figure. The ratio was 45.4 on Jan. 27, its lowest close since September 2011, and has averaged 64.9 this year. The ratio rose quickly in November. It stood at about 77.6 on Nov. 12 and about 82.7 on Nov. 16, analyst Przemyslaw Radomski wrote on FXEmpire, as traders priced in a near-certain Federal Reserve rate increase in December. Since 1968 the ratio has averaged 59.1, and its record high was 123.5 in March 2020, according to Bullion Trading. Newman said Metals Focus remained "longer-term bullish" on gold and silver, Kitco reported, adding that prices "have held up remarkably well with limited institutional exposure." Silver depends more on industrial buyers. body: Crude oil remains under upward pressure from escalating Middle East tensions and concerns about possible supply disruptions. Against this backdrop, West Texas Intermediate (WTI) is little changed near $83.00 per barrel in Friday's Asian trading, following modest gains in the previous session. Missile attacks on Riyadh, Saudi Arabia's capital, were launched on Thursday by the Iran-aligned Houthi movement. At the same time, Iran's navy said two oil tankers had struck naval mines and exploded in the Strait of Hormuz. The incidents intensified concerns about interruptions to transit through the critical shipping route. Signs of substantial production growth and possible market surpluses nevertheless persist despite the regional incidents. According to US Energy Secretary Chris Wright, flows through the Strait of Hormuz have in fact climbed to record levels as Middle Eastern output recovers. Separately, a trilateral agreement to expand the production and supply of refined petroleum products was reached on Thursday by the United States, China, and Russia. For the current quarter, the International Energy Agency forecasts a global supply surplus of roughly 2 million barrels per day. Goldman Sachs has similarly warned of a possible oversupply next year. On Iran, President Donald Trump said he was in no hurry to make a decision, although recent reports indicate an increasing likelihood of further US strikes. Brent remains supported, though growing evidence of looser fundamentals is limiting its upside. Commerzbank analysts report that prices "gained 0.8% to USD 92.68" as market participants continued to "weigh ongoing Middle East shipping disruptions against signs of a broader physical market shift towards surplus,". Among the crude oil varieties traded internationally, WTI, short for West Texas Intermediate, is one of three major types alongside Brent and Dubai Crude. Its relatively low gravity and sulphur content earn it the descriptions “light” and “sweet”, respectively. These characteristics make it a high-quality oil that is easy to refine. Produced in the United States, WTI is distributed through the Cushing hub, known as “The Pipeline Crossroads of the World”. The oil market uses WTI as a benchmark, and its price is regularly cited in the media. Supply and demand primarily determine WTI oil prices, as they do for other assets. Stronger global growth can lift demand, while weaker growth can have the reverse effect. On the supply side, political instability, wars and sanctions can cause disruptions that affect prices. Decisions by OPEC, the group of major oil-producing countries, are another important influence. WTI crude is also sensitive to the US Dollar's value because oil is traded predominantly in US Dollars. A weaker US Dollar can therefore make oil more affordable, while a stronger currency can have the opposite effect. WTI oil prices respond to the weekly oil inventory reports from the American Petroleum Institute (API) and the Energy Information Agency (EIA), as stock movements reflect shifts in supply and demand. Falling inventories may signal stronger demand and push oil prices higher; rising stocks may point to increased supply and weigh on prices. The API releases its report each Tuesday, followed by the EIA the next day. The two sets of findings are generally similar, coming within 1% of one another 75% of the time. As the EIA is a government agency, its figures are regarded as more reliable. At meetings held twice a year, the 12 oil-producing nations belonging to OPEC (Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries) jointly set production quotas for member countries. WTI oil prices frequently react to these decisions: lower quotas can constrain supply and lift prices, whereas increased production has the reverse effect. title: Goldman Sachs sees crude easing to $78 by late 2027 despite ongoing West Asia tensions. Here's why - Business Today
body: Benchmark Brent crude is projected to fall from $93 per barrel to $78 by early December 2027 — and average $88 across the year — as West Asia producers bypass Strait of Hormuz disruptions and push the global oil market into a 2 million barrel-per-day surplus, according to Goldman Sachs Research. The forecast assumes no definitive diplomatic breakthrough in the war in Iran and no re-escalation causing major long-term damage to oil infrastructure. Analysts estimate the market already tipped into surplus in October 2026 after Persian Gulf crude exports climbed 2 million barrels per day from the prior month to recover to their 2025 average. Daan Struyven, co-head of global commodities research and head of oil research at Goldman Sachs, notes that oil prices have risen less sharply than expected given the duration of shipping disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz due to rapid adjustments across supply chains and consumption. “For 2027, we again expect a contest between high supply disruption risk and continued market adaptation,” Struyven wrote in the report released recently. Even as Goldman Sachs projects easing prices later in 2027, analysts caution that volatility remains active. Near-term upside risks include intensified shipping attacks, damage to oil infrastructure, and a rebuilt geopolitical risk premium — alongside potential refinery strikes, heavy planned maintenance, and refiners shifting output from gasoline to diesel, which led Goldman to recommend long positions in European gasoline for summer 2027 as a hedge. Conversely, stronger supply, weaker demand, or a smaller risk premium than assumed could weigh further on prices. International Energy Agency executive director Fatih Birol cautioned that the crisis — which the IEA's World Energy Outlook estimates has caused cumulative losses of 2.8 billion barrels of oil and 60 billion cubic metres of gas — would leave deeper scars the longer it persists, despite producer and consumer resilience. Markets will next watch OPEC+ ministers when they meet on November 29 to weigh 2027 production policy. title: Owens Corning's Stock Slump May Have a Silver Lining for Dividend Investors - TradingView
body: Owens Corning OC is an unlikely candidate to benefit from the flight to safety in the market. Shares of OC are down over 25% in the last three months, and the company's third-quarter earnings report didn't help the bull case. The company missed on the top and bottom lines. The $2.49 billion in net sales was down 7% year over year (YOY). Sales also fell short of the $2.62 billion analysts expected. The story was worse on the bottom line. Adjusted earnings per share (EPS) of $2.44 were 33% lower YOY and well below the $3.06 consensus estimate. Guidance offered little relief. Management expects fourth-quarter revenue of $2 billion to $2.2 billion. It sees adjusted EBITDA margin falling to 10% to 12%. That compares with 20% in Q3 and 17% in the fourth quarter of 2025. The company also declined to give a 2027 forecast, saying results will depend heavily on market conditions. Amid the ongoing drama in the technology sector, investors received dismal news from the housing sector this week. None of it was bullish for investors hoping for a turnaround in Owens Corning stock. On Nov. 17, the National Association of Home Builders (NAHB), in conjunction with Wells Fargo, released its Housing Market Index. Builder confidence fell four points to 25, the lowest reading since April 2012. Also, 46% of builders cut prices, and 68% of builders used sales incentives. Both percentages were the highest since the COVID-19 pandemic. On Nov. 18, data showed that housing starts increased 9.9% in October. However, most of that gain came from apartments, as multifamily starts jumped 25.5%. Meanwhile, single-family permits fell 8.7% to their weakest level since January 2023. Building permits are a forward-looking indicator that suggests demand could remain weak into 2027. Also on Nov. 18, investors got the reading on weekly mortgage applications, which fell 2.3% for the week ending Nov. 13. Purchase applications fell 3% on the week and were down 18% YOY. The average contract rate for a 30-year fixed mortgage rose to 7.35%, a three-week high. Each of these data points aligns with the Owens Corning 10-Q, in which it put "levels of residential and non-residential construction activity" as the lead item on its list of risks to forward guidance. The data undercuts the idea of a quick rebound. A more optimistic read is that the data supports the view that OC’s Q4 guidance reflects the market, not company-specific problems. In the company's Q3 earnings report, Owens Corning reported that its Roofing business maintained a 29% EBITDA margin. Roofing sales fell 16% YOY to $1.04 billion. Segment EBITDA dropped $124 million to $299 million. The company noted that its roofing distributors are expected to continue destocking after a second consecutive year of below-average storm activity. The weak housing market is a piece of that story. Another factor to consider is a storm season that was weaker than forecasts for the second consecutive year. While that's good news for homeowners, it's a headwind for a company that relies on that demand. Rising costs add to the pressure. Management expects inflation to cost more than $100 million YOY in Q4, similar to Q3. Executives noted that inflation and improving demand have historically set up a spring roofing price increase. However, they did not announce one. The OC chart confirmed a death cross signal when the 50-day simple moving average (SMA) crossed underneath the 200-day SMA around Oct. 26. This is generally considered a bearish indicator, and it's more relevant for Owens Corning, which continues to fall after its earnings report. However, as of Nov. 19, the stock is near a level that has acted as support several times in 2026. A break below this level would put a stock price of around $100 in play. If the market is in a broad correction, as some analysts believe, then that's a real possibility. That's not inconsistent with analysts who have a consensus Hold rating on OC.
